disclosures.name: TestMemmoveOverflow
disclosures.signature: unsafe.Slice: length 3221225472 exceeds the maximum slice length of this runtime
disclosures.reason: structural: the test maps 3 GiB of address space at a fixed address (a temporary file mapped over it 64 KiB at a time), builds `unsafe.Slice((*byte)(base), 3<<30)` over it, and copies the slice over itself shifted by one byte in each direction, requiring memmove to move 3 GiB minus one byte both ways. The slice is 3 GiB long. golib's slice<T> and @string are built over CLR arrays and spans, whose length is Int32 (the native-backed slice constructor takes an int, and no CLR array holds 3 GiB), so a slice of that length has no representation here. READING: unsafe.Slice used to reduce the length with int.CreateTruncating, so 3 GiB WRAPPED negative and the test died on `len is negative` (a length of 4 GiB + 5 would have silently become a 5-element slice, which is a real bug and is fixed by the same seat). It now REFUSES BY NAME past the Int32 span length (unsafe.cs SpanLength, coordinator ruling 2026-09-29 11:33): `unsafe.Slice: length 3221225472 exceeds the maximum slice length of this runtime`. The pin is that refusal text; 3221225472 is the test's own constant (3<<30), so it is fixed. One record. PROOF that no managed implementation of the current slice can meet the assertion: the assertion needs an addressable 3 GiB slice, and the representation caps a slice at the Int32 span length. RETIREMENT CANDIDATE, named and NOT planned: an Int64-length slice representation (native-backed slices over a raw address range with a 64-bit length, decoupled from Span<T>); its footprint is every slice consumer and is UNMEASURED, and no seat owns it. MEASURED on linux (P1, claude/p1-unsafe-slice-length on claude/p1-runtime-ifacehash, Release with tiering off, .NET 10.0.12, go1.24.13, the row read by name). Windows and darwin are NOT read by P1; the test is a linux-only source file (memmove_linux_amd64_test.go). RETIRES if a slice can be longer than Int32 elements.

disclosures.name: TestLFStack
disclosures.reason: structural: two pushes then two pops of PersistentAlloc'd nodes; the FIRST pop's `node.data != 43` fires (`no lifo`). LAYOUT. lfstack_test.go builds `MyNode{ LFNode; data int }` in raw memory from PersistentAlloc, hands the same address to the runtime as an *LFNode (LFStackPush and LFStackPop write `next` at offset 0) and reads `data` back through a *MyNode, which relies on Go's rule that an embedded field sits where it is declared: LFNode at offset 0, data at 16. go2cs emits MyNode with the CLR field order `data, ʗLFNode` (read from the runtime.tests.dll metadata, SequentialLayout): the test's own part declares `data`, and the source generator adds the embedded field's storage in a LATER partial part, which the CLR orders after. `next` at offset 0 of the LFNode view therefore overwrites `data`, and a popped node's data reads back a packed pointer. The lock-free stack itself is correct: a probe over three persistentalloc'd lfnodes pushes and pops in LIFO order with correct packing (SIZING-p1-runtime-fixables-2026-09-29.md section 2). PROOF that no golib routine can meet it: the ordering is decided by the CLR's partial-part field order, and the assertion reads the reinterpreted bytes, so nothing the runtime package implements sits between the layout and the read. RETIREMENT CANDIDATE, named and NOT planned (coordinator ruling 2026-09-29 02:57): emit an embedded field's storage in declaration order (converter plus the struct source generator). Its footprint is every struct that embeds a type and declares another field, UNMEASURED, and no seat owns it; an entry that stops matching because the layout changed is the retirement signal, and the entry then leaves the manifest. WINDOWS: the i9's windows census (CENSUS-runtime-endgame-windows-2026-09-29.md, TRAIN I union 9e1594dcd2, rows 2 of section 2) reads the same two texts, `no lifo` and `Wrong sum -4314593837846761957/4950`, so ONE entry with these pins covers both flavours; on windows the packed-pointer round trip already fails without the spanOf answer, and the emission is the same. Windows was read by the i9, not by P1. MEASURED on linux (P1, the P1 union tree (claude/p1-runtime-fixable bdfbd2244f + the refusal cuts + the disclosure seat 7c27acb6c5 + TRAIN I 61cf81290c, P1's measurement merge), linux, Release with tiering off, .NET 10.0.12, go1.24.13, the full 120 m runtime row of that tree, 10,883 verdicts; the six allocation and layout rows read the same counts in the full row of claude/p1-runtime-fixable bdfbd2244f alone). Windows and darwin are NOT read by P1.

disclosures.name: TestNonEscapingMap
disclosures.reason: structural: want-zero AllocsPerRun asserts over four shapes of a map that does not escape (a literal, `make` with no hint, with the constant hint 8, with a variable hint), each followed by `m[0] = 0`. WANT: 0 allocations per run in each. READING: 1 counted object per run in each shape, unit COUNT (1,000 go2cs-runtime object allocations, 232,000 bytes, over 1,000 runs) at the P1 union tree (claude/p1-runtime-fixable bdfbd2244f + the refusal cuts + the disclosure seat 7c27acb6c5 + TRAIN I 61cf81290c, P1's measurement merge), linux, Release with tiering off, .NET 10.0.12, go1.24.13; the first pin is the map-literal arm and the records pin of 5 carries the other three arms and the unit note. PROOF, with the objects Go keeps off the heap NAMED: for a non-escaping map Go's compiler (walkMakeMap) puts the map header (runtime maps.Map) in the caller's frame and, when the hint is at most 8, also the first group of eight slots, so `m[0] = 0` writes into frame memory and mallocs nothing. golib's `map<K,V>` is a readonly struct over a CLR Dictionary, and the store's insert needs that Dictionary's bucket and entry arrays, which are CLR objects. A frame-local form is unavailable because a Go map is a REFERENCE: `m2 := m` and a callee's `m[k] = v` must be visible through every copy, and an inline first group inside a copied struct would fork on the copy. Keeping it off the heap needs the escape fact (no alias outlives the frame) that go2cs does not compute. RETIREMENT CANDIDATE, named and NOT planned (coordinator ruling 2026-09-29 02:57): a non-escaping-map form in DESIGN-nonescaping-locals.md (REC-B) whose first group lives inline in the frame, with the falsifier stated: a golib small-map representation that keeps its first group inline without forking on a copy would read 0 here and retire the entry. Its feasibility and footprint are UNMEASURED. MEASURED on linux (P1, the P1 union tree (claude/p1-runtime-fixable bdfbd2244f + the refusal cuts + the disclosure seat 7c27acb6c5 + TRAIN I 61cf81290c, P1's measurement merge), linux, Release with tiering off, .NET 10.0.12, go1.24.13, the full 120 m runtime row of that tree, 10,883 verdicts; the six allocation and layout rows read the same counts in the full row of claude/p1-runtime-fixable bdfbd2244f alone). Windows and darwin are NOT read by P1.

disclosures.name: TestArrayHash
disclosures.reason: AllocsPerRun-derived assertion in runtime's hash test over fixed arrays: the test hashes [8]string keys through a map and requires at most 6 allocations per run (`too many allocs 326 - hash not balanced`). Go keeps each `var k [8]string` local in the frame and copies a map key by value into the bucket; the converted code allocates the array backing of each local (256 locals per run) and a fresh backing for each of the map-key copies (about 70), which is the 326 objects the counter sees. The unit note is COUNT (`counted 3,260 go2cs-runtime object allocations (977,680 bytes) over 10 runs`): golib's counter SAW the objects, the COUNT arm of the 2026-09-05 ladder. disclosures.name: TestNewOSProc0
disclosures.signature: runtime: clone: goroutines are CLR threads, so a raw clone s
disclosures.reason: runtime-capability: the test calls runtime.NewOSProc0, which allocates a stack and issues a raw `clone` syscall whose child runs a Go function pointer (newOSProcCreated) on a NEW KERNEL THREAD, then waits up to five seconds for the child to set a flag. Goroutines here are CLR threads and a function pointer here is a managed token, not machine code, so a raw clone that starts one has no managed meaning. `clone` is an assembly function, so the generator stubbed it with a NotImplementedException, which the host classifies as an infrastructure-error, a verdict no disclosure can absorb; it now REFUSES BY NAME (runtime/linux/os_linux_impl.cs, this seat, coordinator ruling 2026-09-29 02:57). One assertion; the pin is the refusal text. Scoped to linux: nosan_linux_test.go and os_linux.go are linux files. MEASURED on linux (P1, the P1 union tree (claude/p1-runtime-fixable bdfbd2244f + the refusal cuts + the disclosure seat 7c27acb6c5 + TRAIN I 61cf81290c, P1's measurement merge), linux, Release with tiering off, .NET 10.0.12, go1.24.13, the full 120 m runtime row of that tree, 10,883 verdicts; the six allocation and layout rows read the same counts in the full row of claude/p1-runtime-fixable bdfbd2244f alone). Windows and darwin are NOT read by P1. RETIRES if the host can start a managed function on a new kernel thread through clone; by design it cannot.

disclosures.name: TestSignalM
disclosures.signature: runtime: tgkill: an M here is a CLR thread with no kernel th
disclosures.reason: runtime-capability: the test parks a locked goroutine in WaitForSigusr1 and sends SIGUSR1 to that goroutine's M through signalM, which is tgkill(getpid(), mp.procid, SIGUSR1), then requires the M that received the signal to be the M it was sent to. The host has no kernel thread id per M (procid is never recorded, an M is a CLR thread) and no Go signal handler, so a signal cannot be aimed at one thread. `getpid` answers Environment.ProcessId now (this seat) and `tgkill` REFUSES BY NAME (runtime/linux/os_linux_impl.cs): both were assembly functions stubbed with a NotImplementedException, an infrastructure-error that no disclosure can absorb. The waiting goroutine is left parked in its pipe read when the refusal unwinds the test (inferred from the code, not observed). The pin is the tgkill refusal. Scoped to linux for the same reason as TestNewOSProc0. MEASURED on linux (P1, the P1 union tree (claude/p1-runtime-fixable bdfbd2244f + the refusal cuts + the disclosure seat 7c27acb6c5 + TRAIN I 61cf81290c, P1's measurement merge), linux, Release with tiering off, .NET 10.0.12, go1.24.13, the full 120 m runtime row of that tree, 10,883 verdicts; the six allocation and layout rows read the same counts in the full row of claude/p1-runtime-fixable bdfbd2244f alone). Windows and darwin are NOT read by P1. RETIRES if the host can deliver a signal to one managed thread; by design it cannot.

disclosures.name: TestCallersDeferNilFuncPanicWithLoop
disclosures.reason: structural: the test puts a nil deferred call in a LOOP, which Go compiles as a non-open-coded defer, and requires runtime.Callers from the recovering deferred function to list Go's frames `func1, gopanic, panicmem, sigpanic, deferreturn, test`. The deferreturn frame is the frame of the runtime routine that runs a non-open-coded defer at function exit; the emission's defer model has no such frame, since every defer runs from the one GoFrame.Run in a finally block, so nothing exists to list between sigpanic and the test. R's panic-frames design (ruling a7dc4570d3, 2026-09-27 12:03) splices gopanic, panicmem and sigpanic and KEEPS a disclosure for deferreturn alone ('Disclosure is kept only for deferreturn (the WithLoop form)'); the reading agrees: got `runtime.Callers ...func1 runtime.gopanic runtime.panicmem runtime.sigpanic <test> testing.tRunner`, want the same list with runtime.deferreturn after sigpanic. The pin is the GOT half's adjacency `runtime.sigpanic runtime_test.TestCallersDeferNilFuncPanicWithLoop`, which is the absence of the deferreturn frame and nothing else: the wanted half is the test's own constant and would keep matching, and a run where deferreturn appeared would stop matching here. WINDOWS: the i9's census reads the same wanted list at 9e1594dcd2 (first 200 characters only); P1 did not read windows. MEASURED on linux (P1, the P1 union tree (claude/p1-runtime-fixable bdfbd2244f + the refusal cuts + the disclosure seat 7c27acb6c5 + TRAIN I 61cf81290c, P1's measurement merge), linux, Release with tiering off, .NET 10.0.12, go1.24.13, the full 120 m runtime row of that tree, 10,883 verdicts; the six allocation and layout rows read the same counts in the full row of claude/p1-runtime-fixable bdfbd2244f alone). Windows and darwin are NOT read by P1. RETIRES if the emission ever prints a deferreturn frame for a non-open-coded defer.

disclosures.name: TestTracebackInlined/simple
disclosures.reason: runtime-capability: Go's inliner decides which frames are folded into their caller, and prints an inlined frame's arguments as `(...)`; the test checks both, and its own comment says `This test requires inlining` (it skips when optimization is off). go2cs keeps Go's function boundaries one-for-one and the CLR JIT's inlining is invisible to a managed stack walk that is meant to show Go's frames, so the fold is Go's compiler's decision and cannot be recovered here. Diagnostic-only (the owner's 2026-09-28 principle). Reading: the printed traceback parses (the records' first line is that traceback, which the test logs before it compares), and the compare fails at the first frame that Go prints with `(...)`. WINDOWS: the i9's census (TRAIN I union 9e1594dcd2) reads the same shape (the traceback as the first record); P1 did not read windows. MEASURED on linux (P1, the P1 union tree (claude/p1-runtime-fixable bdfbd2244f + the refusal cuts + the disclosure seat 7c27acb6c5 + TRAIN I 61cf81290c, P1's measurement merge), linux, Release with tiering off, .NET 10.0.12, go1.24.13, the full 120 m runtime row of that tree, 10,883 verdicts; the six allocation and layout rows read the same counts in the full row of claude/p1-runtime-fixable bdfbd2244f alone). Windows and darwin are NOT read by P1. RETIRES if the host prints Go's inline-frame `(...)` marker; by design it does not inline.

disclosures.signature:
got:
redacted.go:0:

redacted.go:0: runtime.gopanic
traceback_system_test.go:100
disclosures.reason: runtime-capability: the test re-execs itself, crashes the child (a panic in /panic, a nil write in /trap) and symbolizes the child's printed crash traceback with the PARENT's own tables, requiring Go's frames `gopanic [panicmem sigpanic] child7 ... child1 func1`. Two independent causes each keep it red. R1 (load-bearing, R's sizing on windows at Release TC0, same built test binary re-run with one environment variable changed per arm): at TC0 the JIT drops Go-kept frames through inlining AND through implicit tail calls, so the child's runtime.Callers keeps 3 of Go's 12 frames (child7, func1, goexit); default tiering keeps all 12, and TC0 with DOTNET_JitNoInline=1 keeps exactly the frames whose call is not in tail position. Which frames exist in optimized CLR code is the JIT's decision, so no scoped marking can restore them, and this is a diagnostic-only crash-traceback assertion (the owner's 2026-09-28 principle). R2 (independent, R's sizing): caller PC tokens are interned per process in first-sight order, so the same binary gives the same frame a different token in the child and in the parent, and the parent cannot symbolize the child's PCs: a child PC names another frame or none. Its retirement direction, per-binary DETERMINISTIC caller tokens keyed on the assembly's position-map records, is queued as a caller-band design item and is not dispatched. Named, not load-bearing: the crash traceback starts at the throw site where Go's starts at gopanic, and the managed printer writes no sp=/fp=/pc= fields (a line without pc= is skipped as an inlined frame, which is why the harness prints one empty frame). READING (linux, this seat): the child's own Callers list holds 3 PCs and the harness reports `got: redacted.go:0: ` (one empty frame), the same failure R measured on windows; R1's per-arm environment readings and R2's token readings are R's, on windows, and P1 did not repeat them. The pin is the measured harness failure, the empty got frame followed by the test's own wanted frames, which are fixed text; the record's first line carries per-run PCs and the child's stdout carries a per-run sentinel, so neither is pinned. MEASURED on linux (P1, the P1 union tree (claude/p1-runtime-fixable bdfbd2244f + the refusal cuts + the disclosure seat 7c27acb6c5 + TRAIN I 61cf81290c, P1's measurement merge), linux, Release with tiering off, .NET 10.0.12, go1.24.13, the full 120 m runtime row of that tree, 10,883 verdicts; the six allocation and layout rows read the same counts in the full row of claude/p1-runtime-fixable bdfbd2244f alone). disclosures.name: TestFunctionAlignmentTraceback
disclosures.signature: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
disclosures.reason: runtime-capability: the test reads the CODE BYTE at a PC, *(*uint8)(unsafe.Pointer(pc)) at symtab_test.go:240, one byte before a caller token, expecting the INT3 alignment filler (0xcc) that the Go linker pads functions with. go2cs has no machine code at a PC: runtime.Caller answers an opaque call-site token from a non-canonical band (runtime/managed_impl.cs s_callerSpanBase, 0x8000_8000_0000_0000, TRAIN C's caller-PC spans 96ce90f997), so no byte exists there to read. The read is refused by golib's minted-address sink guard (ManagedPointerTokens.NamesNoUserMemory, bit 63) as Go's nil-dereference panic on EVERY platform. Before that guard the same read was a caught NullReferenceException on linux, because a non-canonical #GP reports address 0 there, and a FATAL AccessViolation on windows that ended the test host at test F and blanked every later verdict of the row (measured 2026-09-27: bisected to ed9dc138e8, pc = 0x800080000000F7FF printed at the site). Pinned to that panic text on this test alone: any OTHER failure here (the FuncForPC name check, or Frames.Next's Func) is a real defect, not this disclosure.

disclosures.name: TestPinnerConstStringData
disclosures.reason: runtime-capability: the test's own comment states its subject -- 'const string data is not in span'. It asserts that unsafe.StringData of a string LITERAL reads runtime.isPinned == true before, during and after a Pinner.Pin/Unpin, which is true in Go because RODATA is not a heap span: spanOfHeap answers nil and the non-Go-pointer arm answers pinned. golib has no RODATA -- a literal's bytes are a heap byte[] (rooted for the process's life but movable) and unsafe.StringData returns an element reference into it -- so the truthful managed answer for that storage is 'a Go heap object, not pinned', and that is what the row reads on its FIRST assertion, before Pin is ever called. Answering true for storage nothing pinned would be fabrication (this class's anti-laundering clause). A truthful form exists in principle -- literal storage on the Pinned Object Heap plus a registry of literal-backed arrays so isPinned can recognise them -- and is REFUSED as one row's consumer paying a corpus-wide, unpriced allocation-policy change; that form is this entry's rejoin clause. Only the first-assertion arm is pinned: Pin and Unpin on that pointer must still not panic, so a regression in the non-Go-pointer no-op reads as a defect, not as this disclosure. Design and prediction: docs/phase4/DESIGN-runtime-pinner.md section 6.1.

disclosures.name: TestPanicSystemstack
disclosures.reason: host-fatal HANG member (the class was widened to admit a deadline-consuming hang beside a crash, coordinator ruling 2026-09-05, recorded at hostFatalClass in testConversion.go; this row RATIFIED as a member by coordinator ruling 2026-09-05 over C1's Q46 reading). The test re-execs the host with the argument testPanicSystemstackInternal; the child's crash_unix_test.go init() starts one goroutine and then calls testPanicSystemstackInternal on the initializing thread, each meant to print "x\n" and then deadlock on a runtime lock inside systemstack so that a SIGQUIT under GOTRACEBACK=crash prints both blocked stacks. MEASURED (solo, Release+TC0, 3 m deadline; Go=pass): the converted child prints ONE x, because the goroutine started inside init() cannot enter testPanicSystemstackInternal until the CLR type-initializer lock is released by the module initializer it was started from -- and that initializer is deadlocking itself by the test's own design (dotnet-stack: main thread = <Module>..cctor -> initΔ3 -> lock2 spinning; goroutine = Goroutine.Run with no body frame, its thread in a futex wait). Go runs init-started goroutines concurrently with init; the CLR serializes every other thread's first touch of an initializing type behind its constructor. The parent therefore never completes io.ReadFull(pr, 4), never sends SIGQUIT, never reaches its deferred Process.Kill, and consumes the package deadline; the deadline's external SIGKILL orphans a child that a hand-sent SIGQUIT kills at once (its SIGQUIT is unblocked and caught, SigPnd empty). NOT a missing feature: the class censused in the pinned GOROOT (a go statement lexically inside func init()) is 2 production + 2 _test.go files and exactly ONE deadlocks, by its own design -- the semantic remedy (a package init that does not hold the type-initializer lock while it runs) is a converter design question recorded on the board with a population of one, not built ahead of a second case. Withdrawn from BOTH sides by the one --skip/-skip regexp and COUNTED IN DISCLOSED. Retires if a second case ever moves the design.

MEASURED on both sides. Native Go at the pinned go1.23.12 finds the pair at ITERATION 2, minimum delta exactly 320 over 191 of 197 consecutive gaps, because Go's size class for a 320-byte object IS 320 and Go stores no per-object header. The CONVERTED path has a hard floor of 344 with ZERO hits at 320 across 199,999 pairs (i9, mailbox d0687ff2), and 344 is independently DERIVED from the CoreCLR x64 object layout as 8 sync block + 8 method-table pointer + 8 length and padding + 320 payload. Two distinct non-overlapping objects are separated by at least the size of the first, so 320 is below the smallest gap this object model CAN produce and the search cannot terminate. REPRESENTATIONAL rather than unimplemented: the assertion references the FOREIGN system's own heap layout, which a correct port answers differently by construction; the row's other verdicts are exactly what an unbuilt implementation would satisfy, so this is NOT an E3 row exclusion and the row stays in the denominator. disclosures.name: TestCrashWhileTracing
disclosures.reason: host-fatal CRASH member (coordinator ruling 2026-09-07). A crash produces no row to pin, so this is the skip-list kind rather than a disclosure of a failing verdict. FACT ABOUT TODAY'S HOST: the test binary dies on an unrecovered panic in a goroutine at this row -- index 104 of 883 in file order -- and the death SHADOWS every later test, leaving 799 rows UNMEASURED; excluding this row alone raised terminal verdicts from 84 to 104 (i9, measured, ungated vs gated at master 5a27a8972). ROOTED end to end and the root is NOT a host defect: runtime.StartTrace is hand-owned on linux and windows and refuses by name because the CLR has no per-thread g (runtime/<goos>/trace_impl.cs), runtime/trace.Start early-returns on that error BEFORE spawning its writer goroutine so nothing is ever written to the child's stdout, the parent's traceparse.NewReader then fails version.ReadHeader's Fscanf on the "go 1." literal, and t.Fatalf aborts the test BEFORE cmd.Wait(); testenv's t.Cleanup cancels the context, os/exec's watchCtx -- still parked because Wait never drained resultc -- takes ctx.Done() and calls cmd.Cancel, whose else branch t.Logf's after the test has completed, and Go's own testing panics on a post-completion log. Every step from the Fatalf onward is FAITHFUL GO (internal/testenv/exec.go:199 and :205, os/exec/exec.go:772); Go never reaches the failing header read because Go's tracer works. The entry is the UNBLOCK, not the answer: it turns 799 unmeasured rows into measurable ones in one cut, and the tracer capability itself remains open work rather than a settled frontier. RETIRES when the test re-admitted produces a terminal verdict. AMENDMENT 2026-09-13 (C1) -- THE 1-6/7-8 MARKING, ruled at f5b35f351 as one dated amendment to be written only once i9's item-4 tail was in. LINKS 1-6 OF THE CHAIN ABOVE ARE READ: source-read at named lines on both sides (runtime/<goos>/trace_impl.cs, runtime/trace/trace.cs, internal/trace/reader.go, crash_test.go). LINKS 7-8 -- testenv's t.Cleanup cancel reaching os/exec's parked watchCtx, and the cmd.Cancel else-branch t.Logf that Go's own testing panics on -- were marked CONSEQUENCE-NOT-MEASURED: a reading of the code's own consequence, not a run. THE TAIL IS IN AND IT DOES NOT MEASURE THEM AT THIS ROW: i9 0dd133719 on landed master 44f858717 (Release, tiered false, .NET 10.0.11, rc=1, 169 s) reaches 185 of 880 verdicts with 695 never reached, and this row is not among them. NOR CAN ANY RUN MEASURE THEM HERE, IN EITHER CONFIGURATION, AND THAT IS THE FINDING RATHER THAN A GAP: run SOLO, the row's cleanup fires while the test is still live, so the late log cannot happen -- measured 2026-09-06, the row fails cleanly in 2.33 s and the host lives (src/tests/GolibTests/LogAfterCompleteTests.cs:34-39, which names this row as the WRONG instrument for exactly this reason); run FULL, this entry's own name enters hostFatalSkipExpression's regexp (src/go2cs/testConversion.go:6600) and withdraws the row from both sides. The entry forecloses its own confirming measurement. WHAT IS MEASURED is links 7-8's TERMINAL SHAPE, at the next door rather than this one: TestLockOSThreadNesting dies on "panic: Log in goroutine after TestLockOSThreadNesting has completed", thrown at src/core/testing/TestExecution.cs:418 after the ancestor walk at :407 finds no live ancestor (root-read by C1 at 18a34299f; the walk is Go's logDepth shape, landed 1aff2a352 and an ancestor of the tail's own tree) -- the same post-completion-log kill links 7-8 describe, and faithful, since Go panics on that condition too. SO THE MARKING STANDS AS: 1-6 READ; 7-8 READ AND MECHANISM-CONFIRMED AT A SIBLING DOOR, NEVER MEASURED AT THIS ROW, AND NOT MEASURABLE AT IT. Nothing above this amendment changes, the RETIRES trigger included.

disclosures.name: TestSetPanicOnFault
disclosures.reason: host-fatal CRASH member (coordinator ruling 2026-09-26, the P1 host-fatal seat). runtime_test.go sets debug.SetPanicOnFault(true) and then reads one byte through (*byte)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) for each of the 19 faultAddrs (0, 1, 0xfff and 16 high kernel or malformed addresses), recovering each fault as a panic and failing only if none faulted. Go turns the SIGSEGV into a recoverable panic; the CLR does not. MEASURED on linux (P1, the stack 959a88df3 plus the metrics-histogram fix 0a074655e, Release, tiered off): the host dies with "Fatal error. System.AccessViolationException: Attempted to read or write protected memory" at ж<byte>.op_OnesComplement inside testSetPanicOnFault, no verdict is written, and every later test in the phase is lost. .NET treats an access violation as a corrupted-state fault that managed code cannot catch, so there is no managed refusal to prefer over a skip here: the fault happens inside the read, not in any runtime function that could refuse first. Which of the addresses faulted first is NOT measured (the test logs an address only after a read succeeds). Windows and darwin are NOT measured; the entry carries no platforms field because the uncatchable access violation is a property of the CLR on every target, which is inferred, not read. runtime/debug's TestPanicOnFault is the same fault class and the first member of this class. Withdrawn from BOTH sides by the one --skip/-skip regexp and COUNTED IN DISCLOSED. RETIRES when the managed runtime can recover a hardware fault as a panic.

disclosures.name: TestUserArenaLiveness/Free
disclosures.signature: expected arena-referenced object to be finalized
disclosures.reason: the test gives an arena object v a pointer to a heap object with a finalizer, drops v (`v = nil`), frees the arena (or, in /Finalizer, drops it), and then requires that finalizer to run, from inside the same still-running frame. Go's per-safepoint liveness maps drop v at its last use; the CLR reports the slots of a frame with exception handling (the converted defer's try/finally) live for the frame's whole lifetime, so v and everything it references stay rooted while the test is looking. The arena itself releases everything it allocated (arena_impl.cs, C2 C3 USER ARENAS). Measured on linux, Release, tiered off, as a one-axis A/B over the frame alone: the identical sequence (allocate smallPointerMix through UserArena.New, set its C to a fresh heap object, SetFinalizer on it, Free, runtime.GC() twice) run behind a RETURNED NoInlining call leaves v, v.C and the arena all collected (weak references dead), while inline in the test frame v and v.C stay alive even with the test's `x` and `v` explicitly cleared and v held past the clearing store. GolibTests' RuntimeUserArenaTests.AnObjectReachableOnlyFromTheArenaLivesUntilFree guards the arena half. The same class as runtime/debug's TestFreeOSMemory. RETIRES when the host reports frame liveness per safepoint, or the converter can end a local's lifetime at its last use.

disclosures.name: TestUserArenaLiveness/Finalizer
disclosures.signature: expected arena-referenced object to be finalized
disclosures.reason: Same frame-liveness retention as TestUserArenaLiveness/Free, with the arena dropped instead of freed (its handle unreachable after `arena = nil`): the arena and its allocation list are collected, and v, still reported live by the test frame, keeps the finalizer's object alive. Measured in the same A/B as /Free.
